The investigations have also addressed the trade-offs between BEV vehicle range (specifically battery capacity and the ability to add additional charge during service activity), charging parameters, power availability, and operations predictability with respect to policy and infrastructure configurations. In addition, Phase III research has examined the criticality of station operations, also referred to as curb management depending on the reference context. Lessons and insights from simulations of automated transit network (ATN) studies inform principles of station design for robust AMD operation. Configuration and management of a given transport system’s boarding and alighting stations (often called pickup and drop-off [PUDO] zones) and their impact on overall system throughput and performance are analyzed. The integration of electrification into stations and the use of infrastructure intelligence within station/curbfront boarding zones have also been addressed. Finally, findings and conclusions have been drawn from Phase III research with respect to system integration and analysis needs for AMDs. This forms the basis for what is proposed as a systems engineering methodology (SEM) necessary to adequately define the resilience and sustainability of mobility systems and their infrastructure within any large-scale AMD implementations that are anticipated to occur over the next 5–10 years. 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 The Concept of an Automated Mobility District Over the past 2 centuries, our modern society has been continuously trending toward the concentration of residential, business, and entertainment developments within dense urban settings as we evolved from a primarily agrarian society to industrialization—and now to an information-centric economy. In turn, this concentration of our population toward major urban districts has also been accompanied by similar densification of major activity centers such as medical centers and university campuses, sports and entertainment complexes, and airports and major intermodal transportation hubs. A new dynamic has appeared in this evolution of our urban lifestyles as technology transforms the way we move to, from, and within these dense urban settings. The research endeavors discussed throughout this report refer to this urban transformation as forming AMDs, where automated mobility technologies are envisioned to replace multiple manually driven forms of mobility—primarily the private automobile—providing safer and more time-, energy-, and space-efficient transport to enhance our quality of life. Within these AMDs, transport by a variety of modes would comprise primary modes, facilitating readily accessible movement throughout the district. Access to automated modes will minimize reliance on privately owned vehicles for most local trips, freeing up valuable real estate otherwise allocated for private vehicle storage to instead be used for more efficient and denser development while relieving the mobility system users of the overhead of maintaining, operating, and parking a vehicle. 2.1 Functional Definition of an Automated Mobility District The first edition of the AMD catalog defined an automated mobility district as follows: a geographically confined district or campus-sized implementation of connected and automated vehicle technology for the purpose of publicly accessible
